titleText.es: Eso sí, no esperéis ninguna indulgencia con las multas por atrasos en la devolución
titleText.en: That said, don't expect any leniency with fines for late returns.

regions.labelEs: VENTAJAS DE SALIR CON UNA BIBLIOTECARIA

applications.explanationEn: Ventajas names the benefits, de introduces the activity, and salir stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Salir gains the dating meaning because con introduces a person, here una bibliotecaria.

regions.labelEs: VAMOS A PARAR EN BALTIMORE PARA VISITAR A MI FAMILIA Y NO HAY MÁS QUE HABLAR.

applications.explanationEn: Vamos matches “we,” a connects the pieces, and parar stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Para introduces the purpose of the stop, and visitar stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
A appears because the people being visited are the specific family identified by mi.
No hay denies that any further discussion exists, while más que hablar names that possible additional discussion.
Ah marks the reaction and sí echoes the claim being challenged; question intonation turns the pair into a skeptical response.

regions.labelEs: EH, MIRA, ¡ES UN LIBRO DE TAPA DURA NUEVO!

applications.explanationEn: Mira directly tells one familiar person to look, using the ordinary positive tú command form.
Libro names the object, de links it to the cover type, and dura agrees with the feminine word tapa.
Nuevo comes after the complete noun phrase headed by libro and describes the book as new.
The action is left unstated because the situation makes it obvious; the direct challenge turns the literal statement about ability into a dare.
Serás keeps the full dictionary form ser and adds the future ending -ás for informal singular “you.”
Ganas already identifies informal singular “you,” while tú adds contrast by emphasizing that the other person wins.

cards.questionEn: How do you introduce the advantages of doing an activity?
cards.answerEn: Use ventajas de followed by the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The action verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and names the activity whose benefits are being discussed.

example.es: Hablamos de las ventajas de caminar.
example.en: We are talking about the advantages of walking.

cards.answerEn: to date; to go out with (in salir con)
cards.noteEn: Salir by itself usually means “to go out” or “to leave.” With con followed by a person, it can mean to date that person.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is dating another person?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of salir, then con, then the person.
cards.noteEn: This relationship meaning depends on con plus a person. In other settings, salir can simply mean “to go out” or “to leave.”

cards.answerEn: we are going; we are going to
cards.noteEn: Vamos is the present form of ir for “we.” Before a and an action verb, it can announce a plan or near-future action.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of ir (“to go”), then a, then the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Ir changes to match the person: voy a means “I am going to,” vas a means “you are going to,” and va a means “he/she is going to.” The final action stays in its unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form. This pattern expresses a plan, intention, or expected future event.
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is going to do something?

cards.answerEn: to (part of ir a + infinitive, going to do something)
to stop; to make a stop
Use para followed by the verb’s dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Use para + verb when the same person or thing performs both actions: in estudio para aprender, I both study and learn. When someone else performs the second action, Spanish needs the different pattern para que.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “in order to do something” in Spanish?

example.en: I study in order to learn.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks a specific person as the object
cards.noteEn: Spanish generally places a before a specific person who receives a verb’s action. This “personal a” is not translated as a separate English word.

cards.promptEs: a + persona o expresión que se refiere a una persona
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish sometimes put a before the person affected by an action?
cards.answerEn: Put a before a person—or a word such as alguien or nadie—when that person directly receives the action.
cards.noteEn: This a is called the personal a. It is common before a named or specific person, but person-denoting words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) also take it. English usually has no separate word for it. Before the masculine article el, a + el contracts to al.

cards.questionEn: How do you say firmly that there is nothing more to discuss?
cards.answerEn: Use no hay más que hablar.
cards.noteEn: The expression closes a discussion by presenting the decision as final. Más means “more,” while que links it to hablar, the remaining possible discussion.

example.es: La decisión está tomada; no hay más que hablar.
example.en: The decision is made; there is nothing more to discuss.

cards.answerEn: to; no separate word (in no hay más que hablar)

cards.noteEn: Ah can signal recognition, surprise, or a challenge. In ¿Ah, sí?, the speaker questions what was just said, much like “Oh, really?”

cards.questionEn: How do you react with a skeptical or challenging “Oh, really?”
cards.noteEn: The same two words can sound genuinely surprised or openly challenging; the speaker's tone and the situation supply the difference.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “hardcover book” in Spanish?
cards.noteEn: Spanish builds the description literally as a book “of hard cover.” De links the book to its cover type, and dura agrees with the feminine noun tapa.

example.es: Compré un libro de tapa dura.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links an item to its type
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between an item and the noun that identifies its type. English often puts the type noun first instead: libro de historia becomes “history book.”

cards.promptEs: no ser capaz (de + infinitivo) · como reto
cards.questionEn: How can you challenge someone by implying that they would not dare or be able to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use no, a form of ser, and capaz, often followed by de and the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The literal meaning is “not be capable,” but said directly to someone it can function as a dare. The action may be left unstated when the situation makes it obvious.
Serás is the simple-future form of ser for informal singular “you.” Spanish writes an accent on the final -ás.

example.en: You will be a good guide.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone will do in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Keep the action verb in its dictionary form and add a future ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The ending identifies the person: sentir plus -á gives sentirá, and ver plus -á gives verá. A few common verbs change their stem, but use the same endings.

cards.questionEn: Why might Spanish say tú or yo when the verb already tells you who acts?
cards.answerEn: Say the subject pronoun to add emphasis, contrast, or clarity; otherwise Spanish often leaves it out.
cards.noteEn: A verb form such as eres already points to “you.” Adding tú can stress that particular person, especially in a contrast or a surprised question. The pronoun may appear after the verb.
